Michael Saylor has had a tough year. It just got tougher. Index provider MSCI is moving to drop Strategy (MSTR), Saylor's Bitcoin-hoarding company, from its global standard index.

MSTR stock is down 11% at the time of writing.

MCSCI said on Thursday it would classify "non-operating companies" as ineligible for inclusion in the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes. It reiterated that "investment funds, business development companies (BDCs)" and "other passive investment vehicles" were a no-go. The rule also covers "other corporate issuers with similar characteristics identified through new quantitative screens." The announcement doesn't name any company, but you get the drift that it's pointed at Strategy.

With roughly 1,500 employees, Strategy is technically an operating company, so it doesn't fit MSCI's first category. It can only get caught by the screens (its pass-or-fail test) in the second asking whether an issuer is a company with substantial operating assets. Bitcoin is obviously Strategy's dominant operating asset as the flywheel would certainly not work without it.

Saylor thinks otherwise, but that's nothing new. The company's main rebuttal is its second-quarter 10-Q, filed August 3, which Strategy argues shows its bitcoin treasury is a separate operating segment, not a passive holding. This is likely tied to STRC, but unpacking that logic would be another post. Strategy also records bitcoin gains and losses as operating expenses.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

SCI saves the knockout punch for the end. Starting with its November 2026 Index Review, it will scrap the interim measures covering companies whose digital asset holdings make up 50% or more of total assets. That's Strategy. In case anyone missed it, Strategy sits at the top of MSCI's attached list of potentially affected securities. Japan's Metaplanet and uranium investor Yellow Cake made the list too.

So… what does this mean for MSTR holders? Well, potentially almost $3 billion in outflows, according to JPMorgan analyst Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou in a November 2025 report. If other indexes follow suit, $8.8 billion. That's not great for shareholders, already down over 50% the past year.

Saylor didn't seem all that worried Friday morning. He went on Bloomberg wearing his infamous orange tie, claimed bitcoin was at the beginning of a bull market and noted "banking adoption" acceleration and the general bullishness of the digital asset space.

MSCI is set to release the final list of affected companies on November 11. The new rules will then take effect after the market closes on November 30.

Dutch Bros (NYSE: BROS) is struggling. At least, that's the way it looks when you're checking out its stock chart. The coffee chain's share price is down 33% year-to-date as of Oct. 16. At the same time, Dutch Bros is doing pretty much everything right.

Is the fast-growing coffee stock a good buy right now?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Brewing up strong results

I'm not kidding about the company's business performance.

Dutch Bros keeps beating analyst expectations across the board in every earnings report, often by a wide margin.

Trailing sales are up 58% over the last three years. The store count increased by 62% to 1,225 locations over the same period. Diluted earnings per share? Up 142%. Free cash flow tripled.

Same-store sales also tick up in almost every report, including a 3.8% year-over-year jump in Q2 2026.

And the founder-led management team has a very specific growth plan. Dutch Bros should have 2,029 stores in the year 2029. Beyond that punny target, the company could reach 7,000 domestic stores before looking for international growth.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
What makes Dutch Bros different

Dutch Bros backs up its strong results and ambitious plans with concrete business advantages.

Customer-friendly baristas are kind of expected at every coffee shop, but an outgoing personality is a written requirement for this company's "broistas." A wide variety of flavoring syrups and toppings lets every customer create their own dream drink. In hot, humid states or seasons, the company sells a ton of energy refreshers and blended freeze coffees -- cold drinks for a warm day.

And the company's focus on the drive-through experience brings another important advantage. The shops don't come with sit-down dining areas that require cleaning and maintenance. Furthermore, the resulting tiny footprint makes the store construction a bit faster and cheaper. The network would expand much more slowly if Dutch Bros insisted on cozy sit-downs in the Starbucks style.

Time to grab a cup of Dutch Bros?

So yes, it's time to buy this stock. Dutch Bros is doing everything right except pleasing the stock market. The business keeps firing on all cylinders, and the market is handing out a 33% discount on a long-term growth story.
